extracted.intended_audience: researchers, meta-researchers, journal editors, and peer reviewers in biomedical research
extracted.subtask_description: Methods and criteria for identifying, categorizing, measuring, and reporting 'spin' (biased interpretation or presentation of results) in published biomedical studies across study designs. Includes definitions, instruments, outcomes, coder procedures, examples of spin practices, and suggested safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of spin (four inductive categories)
rubrics_metrics.description: Spin defined as reporting practices that distort interpretation and create misleading, more favourable conclusions; discordance between results and a more favourable interpretation; attribution of causality when design does not permit it; and overinterpretation or inappropriate extrapolation of results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors inductively classified definitions into 4 categories used by included reports: (1) reporting practices that distort interpretation and create misleading conclusions; (2) discordance between results and their interpretation with the interpretation more favourable than results; (3) attribution of causality when the study design does not allow it; (4) overinterpretation/inappropriate extrapolation. Note: the exclusive use of causal language in observational/nonrandomised studies was commonly treated as spin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spin-related outcomes to measure
rubrics_metrics.description: Key measurable outcomes used in studies of spin: prevalence of spin; level/severity of spin; specific practices used to spin results; factors associated with spin; and impact of spin on reader interpretation or decision-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevalence was the most common outcome (measured in abstracts, main texts, and sometimes titles). Level/severity measures were less common and often used validated instruments (e.g., Boutron). Investigators should state which of these outcomes they measure and report numerator/denominator (x/n, percentage) and summary statistics (median, range) by study type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of prespecified, standardized instruments and validation
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess spin using prespecified standardized data collection instruments (e.g., Boutron et al. instrument) where possible, and report any pilot or reliability testing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the review 94% of reports used a prespecified instrument; 26% used/adapted the Boutron instrument originally for RCTs with nonsignificant primary outcomes. Many used author-generated instruments; only a minority reported pilot/reliability testing (32% of those assessing spin). Recommendation: prefer validated instruments, or if using author-generated tools, report piloting, interrater reliability, and how items were derived (inductive vs. deductive).

rubrics_metrics.name: Boutron instrument high-level spin criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'high' level of spin in study conclusions is defined as: no uncertainty in framing of conclusions; no recommendations for further trials; no acknowledgment of statistically nonsignificant primary outcomes; and/or making recommendations to use the intervention in clinical practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This definition (from Boutron et al.) has been widely applied in assessing severity of spin in trials with nonsignificant primary outcomes. Use these explicit markers to rate severity when applicable; report separate prevalence for 'high' spin in abstracts vs main text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment procedures: independent coding, discrepancy resolution, and blinding
rubrics_metrics.description: Use multiple independent data extractors/coders to assess spin, and reduce interpretation bias through consensus processes, third-party adjudication, or blinding to study metadata.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common procedures in included reports: two independent coders; resolving discrepancies by discussion until consensus (65%); third reviewer adjudication (29%); occasional blinding of coders to author/funding/journal (6%). These methods should be reported and justified given the subjectivity of spin assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locations of assessment (abstract, main text, title)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess spin in specific parts of the article (abstract, main text, and/or title) and report location-specific prevalence because spin in abstracts/titles may have greater practical impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Half of reports assessed both abstract and main text; some assessed abstract only (21%), main text only (26%), and a few assessed titles (9%). Report and compare discordance between abstract and main text conclusions where relevant; note that spin in abstracts may be more consequential as many clinicians rely on abstracts alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories of spin practices (four thematic categories)
rubrics_metrics.description: Spin practices can be thematically grouped into: (1) inappropriate claims; (2) inappropriate extrapolations or recommendations for clinical practice; (3) selective reporting; (4) more robust or favourable data presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these categories to classify observed spin practices across study designs. They are useful pedagogically for editors/reviewers and can underpin instrument development applicable across research types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inappropriate interpretation given study design (causal claims and false equivalence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific spin practice: making claims inappropriate for the study design, e.g., attributing causality in observational studies or interpreting nonsignificant superiority trials as showing equivalence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include use of causal language in nonrandomised studies (e.g., 'X increases Y') and interpreting nonsignificant results as 'two treatments equally good' when trial was designed for superiority. Flag and code use of causal statements and equivalence claims inconsistent with design and analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inappropriate extrapolations or premature clinical recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific spin practice: making recommendations for clinical practice or expressing unwarranted confidence in interventions/tests without appropriate supporting evidence or without calling for confirmatory trials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In observational/interventional research, note whether authors recommend clinical use or fail to recommend further RCTs where appropriate. The review found many observational studies recommending practice change without indicating need for RCTs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selective reporting and 'cherry picking' outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific spin practice: selectively reporting or emphasizing significant secondary/subgroup results while omitting nonsignificant primary endpoints from abstracts or conclusions to distract readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify omissions of nonsignificant endpoints in abstracts/conclusions that appear in methods/results, selective citation of external research, and disproportionate emphasis on favorable secondary analyses. Quantify discordance between methods/results and abstract/conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: More robust or favourable data presentation (rhetorical tactics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific spin practice: presenting results in an overly optimistic or misleading manner (e.g., overstating strength, describing nonsignificant trends, underreporting adverse events, or misleadingly describing study design as more robust).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: optimistic abstracts, extensive rationales to explain away nonsignificance, failure to discuss complications/risks, and underreporting harms. Code for these rhetorical tactics and compare reported harms/limitations vs. data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors hypothesised and tested for association with spin
rubrics_metrics.description: Common factors examined for association with presence of spin include conflicts of interest and funding source, author characteristics, journal characteristics, and study design/quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The evidence in included reports was heterogeneous and inconclusive for most factors. Researchers should predefine which factors to test, report analytic methods, and account for heterogeneity when synthesizing across studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical finding: nonsignificant primary endpoints associated with spin
rubrics_metrics.description: Across several studies the only consistent positive association with spin was presence of a nonsignificant primary endpoint (i.e., studies with nonsignificant primary outcomes were more likely to exhibit spin).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a key risk marker: focus spin-assessment efforts on trials with nonsignificant primary outcomes. However, heterogeneity limits precise quantification; report context (trial type, bias risk).

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical finding: industry funding not consistently associated with spin
rubrics_metrics.description: Meta-analysis of available studies found industry-sponsored studies were no more likely to contain spin than non-industry sponsored studies (RR 1.08; 95% CI 0.87–1.34 in pooled analysis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume industry funding is a reliable predictor of spin based on current evidence; continue to assess funding/conflict of interest but treat as one of multiple hypothesised factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative synthesis and heterogeneity handling
rubrics_metrics.description: When combining association data across studies, report statistical heterogeneity (I^2) and choose an appropriate meta-analytic model (fixed- or random-effects) justified by heterogeneity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review used I^2 to assess heterogeneity and used a fixed-effect model where applied. Given diverse measures/instruments for spin, carefully consider whether pooling is appropriate and report heterogeneity and sensitivity analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inductive vs prespecified approaches to instrument development
rubrics_metrics.description: Two approaches: prespecifying spin practices to assess (deductive) vs using inductive methods to explore and derive spin practices from the literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most studies used prespecified items; few used inductive methods. Authors recommend more inductive/exploratory work to capture the full diversity of spin across designs and fields before locking into narrow prespecified instruments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended safeguards to prevent spin in publications
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical safeguards: peer reviewers and editors should check consistency between results and conclusions, look for inappropriate causal language and overgeneralisation; guideline developers should base recommendations on systematic reviews; promote open data and multiple independent interpretations; and address structural incentives in academia that promote positive findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial checks should explicitly include spin criteria (e.g., causal claims in observational designs, omission of nonsignificant primary outcomes). Encourage journals to require author statements addressing concordance between results and conclusions, and consider tools/checklists for reviewers to detect spin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measuring impact of spin on readers and decision-making
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether spin affects readers' interpretation, perceived benefit/risk, or downstream decisions (e.g., clinical uptake), ideally via RCTs or studies comparing published reports with regulatory reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence is sparse but shows spin can increase perceived benefit and interest in reading full text; only limited studies link spin to decision changes. Recommend experimental studies (e.g., randomized presentation of spun vs. unspun abstracts) and comparison with regulatory assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting and transparency standards for spin studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Report search strategy, inclusion/exclusion criteria, instrument development/piloting, interrater reliability, exact prevalence numerators/denominators by location and study type, and how definitions/categories of spin were derived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review followed PRISMA methods; investigators assessing spin should similarly be transparent and provide data (e.g., extracted 'findings' verbatim) to permit replication and meta-research synthesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendations for future research on spin
rubrics_metrics.description: Future work should develop comprehensive reproducible measures of spin across study designs, use inductive methods to capture diverse practices, investigate contextual/cultural drivers of spin, and evaluate its impact on research, practice, and policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize instrument validation across fields, experiments on reader interpretation, and studies of systemic incentives that promote spin; report limitations and generalisability explicitly.
